source: MIT 18.06 Linear Algebra, Lecture 1 (Gilbert Strang), ~6-13 min
keypoints: The row picture of a 2x2 system draws each equation as a line; the solution is the point where the two lines meet.
The example system is 2x - y = 0 and -x + 2y = 3, whose solution is x = 1, y = 2.
The line 2x - y = 0 passes through the origin because (0,0) satisfies the equation.
The line -x + 2y = 3 does not pass through the origin; when y = 0 it passes through x = -3.
Checking the solution x = 1, y = 2 in the second equation gives -1 + 4 = 3.
The column picture rewrites the system as x times column one (2, -1) plus y times column two (-1, 2) equals the right-hand side (0, 3).
A linear combination means multiplying columns (vectors) by numbers and adding the results.
The linear combination of columns is described as the most fundamental operation in the whole course.
Solving the system means finding the right amounts (coefficients) that combine the column vectors to produce the right-hand side vector.
The right linear combination here is x = 1 of column one plus y = 2 of column two, producing (0, 3).
In the column-picture drawing, column one is the vector (2, -1) and column two is the vector (-1, 2).
